analysis.one_liner: Shields franchise chains from being treated as joint employers when they require worker-training and safety policies.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the Senate labor committee without a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: Under federal wage, labor, and workplace-safety laws, workers can sometimes hold both their direct employer and the parent brand that controls the business accountable. This bill says certain brand-imposed activities — requiring training on harassment, discrimination, or workplace violence, mandating related policies, or providing protective equipment during the COVID-19 pandemic — could never be used to establish that the parent brand is a joint employer. It would also override any state law that says otherwise.
analysis.who_benefits: Large franchisors — national fast-food, hotel, retail, and other franchise chains — gain a shield: even if they dictate training, harassment and discrimination policies, or pandemic-era safety rules to franchisees, those actions could not be used to hold the brand jointly liable for a franchisee's wage violations, labor-law violations, or safety failures. Small franchise owners also gain some legal clarity.

how_it_helps.text: The bill creates a safe harbor: a franchisor requiring training or policies on sexual harassment, workplace violence, discrimination, human trafficking, apprenticeships, childcare, or paid leave — or providing protective equipment during the COVID-19 pandemic — may not, alone or in combination with any other factor, be treated as an employer of the franchisee or its workers under the National Labor Relations Act, the Fair Labor Standards Act, or the Occupational Safety and Health Act.
The bill preempts state laws that are inconsistent with this safe harbor, so a state could not count those same brand-directed activities toward joint-employer status.

analysis.who_pays: Franchise employees bear the cost. If a franchisor sets the policies but a franchisee commits wage theft, retaliation, or safety violations, workers would have a harder time reaching the parent brand with far deeper pockets, since the brand's involvement in these areas would be carved out of joint-employer analysis. State-level worker protections that reach further would be overridden.

drawbacks.text: The safe harbor covers not just harmless administrative guidance but a franchisor's policy mandates and its right to receive reports of violations — exactly the kinds of control that joint-employer doctrine is designed to weigh when deciding who is accountable for workers' wages and safety.

By preempting state law, the bill would override state approaches that make franchisors answerable for conditions in their branded locations, reducing remedies available to workers in states with stronger protections.

The bill's title frames the covered activities as socially good, but the operative effect is to exclude those activities from the legal test for employer status, which weakens enforcement under the NLRA, FLSA, and OSHA rather than requiring any new training or protection.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill gives franchise chains a predictable boundary against joint-employer liability, which some small franchise owners would welcome as legal clarity. But the trade runs against workers: the parent brands that increasingly dictate workplace practices would be insulated from accountability for wage, labor, and safety violations in those areas, and state protections would be preempted. Because it applies under three major worker-protection statutes and 'alone or in combination with any other factor,' the carve-out is broader than the wholesome-sounding title suggests.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never acted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Mike Braun (R-IN) introduced the bill on March 30, 2023, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
No senator cosponsored the bill, and no further action — no hearing, markup, or floor vote — was taken before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Franchise workers and labor-law enforcement are better off that the bill died, since the joint-employer shield it would have created never became law. No group gained anything from the bill itself.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Franchise workers, who kept existing protections

for.name: Sen. Mike Braun
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and shepherded its referral to the Senate labor committee.

sides.party_line_note: No senator joined as a cosponsor and no vote was ever taken, so the partisan shape of support or opposition was never tested; the bill simply drew no visible support beyond its sponsor.

industries.industry: Franchise chains (fast food, hotels, retail, services)
industries.note: The bill would have made the activities franchisors already use to control franchise workplaces — mandated training, policies, and violation reporting — legally irrelevant to joint-employer status under the NLRA, FLSA, and OSHA, reducing their exposure when franchisees violate wage or safety laws. Workers at branded locations would pay the price in lost accountability.

Franchisees would gain some legal clarity about which brand-directed activities do not make them and the franchisor one employer. The practical benefit is modest, since the safe harbor does not change their own obligations to workers.
